The kamale ngoni is a smaller variant of the ngoni of Mali in West Africa, a chordophone, H-S 323.1. Its body is made of wood or gourd and covered with a dried animal skin, usually goatskin; this type uses a gourd resonator, originally had six strings and later grew to eight to eighteen, and is traditionally tuned pentatonically. It is a fourth above the donso ngoni, with a range of about an octave or a little more. Within the ngoni family, Mande griots play the fasa at celebrations and special occasions, the donso ngoni is mostly used at the ceremonies of the Wasulu hunters' bardic class, and the kamale ngoni became popular in Wasulu, driving the rise of Wasulu music.
卡瑪萊恩貢尼為弦鳴樂器，可奏快速旋律。傳統調音多用五聲音階，亦有演奏者改用七聲音: The kamale ngoni is a chordophone and can play fast melodies. Traditional tuning is mostly pentatonic, though some players use a seven-note scale. It is smaller than the donso ngoni and about a fourth higher. A beginner can first tune it pentatonically, then play fast melodies against singing; in Wasulu music it is often used with voices and the karagnan. The source does not describe how the instrument is held.

Its resonator is usually a gourd, unlike the wooden body of the traditional lute-type ngoni. 恩貢尼至少於1352年已存在，伊本·白圖泰在曼薩·穆薩宮廷見其存在；1620年代: The ngoni existed by at least 1352, when Ibn Battuta saw it at the court of Mansa Musa; in the 1620s Richard Jobson mentioned that the hunters' ngoni was the most used in the Gambia. After enslaved Mande people were taken to North America, the ngoni is thought to have developed into the banjo. The kamale ngoni is said to have been created in Mali around the 1950s and 1960s by Alata Brulaye, and it later became popular in Wasulu, driving the rise of Wasulu music in the 1970s and 1990s; its predecessor, the hunters' ngoni, had six strings, and the kamale ngoni later grew to eight, ten, twelve, fourteen, sixteen and eighteen.
